data.description:
## The defect

`rebar-observability.service` does not publish sparsely. It is **killed part-way through every run**,
and the metrics emitted after the kill point are never published at all.

From the host journal, 2026-09-05:

    18:25:50  Starting rebar-observability.service - rebar health + disk observability probe...
    18:29:50  rebar-observability.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=15/TERM
    18:29:50  rebar-observability.service: Failed with result 'timeout'.
    18:29:50  rebar-observability.service: Consumed 34.131s CPU time.

`systemctl show` gives `TimeoutStartUSec = 4min`. The run above spans **exactly** 18:25:50 -> 18:29:50.
It is not finishing late; it is being SIGTERM-ed on the timeout.

**Frequency: 8 timeout failures in a 40-minute window** — i.e. essentially every run, since the timer
fires about every 5 minutes.

## The decisive measurement: 4 minutes wall-clock, ~35 seconds CPU

Consumed CPU across observed runs: **34.131s** and **39.687s**, against 4 minutes of wall time. So the
probe spends roughly **3.4 minutes BLOCKED**, not computing. This is an I/O stall, not a slow script.

That distinction matters for the fix: raising the timeout would only move the kill point, and making
the script computationally faster would not help at all.

Prime suspect, stated as a LEAD: `docker_du_bytes` runs `du -sx --block-size=1` over the Docker root.
That tree holds ~1.88M files, and a `du` over it under I/O contention is exactly a multi-minute
blocking call with near-zero CPU. This host has documented IOPS-saturation history
(`smudgeless-friendless-longspur`), and an operator `du` on the same tree had to be abandoned for
running long earlier the same day. Confirm before fixing — `GIT_TRACE`-style timing or a per-section
stopwatch will name the blocking call.

## Why this is the root cause of several open tickets, not a new symptom

Metrics are published SEQUENTIALLY as the script proceeds, so where a metric sits in the script
decides whether it survives the kill:

- `root_disk_used_percent` (early) — newest datapoint **18:25Z**, 10 points in 60 min. Healthy.
- `mem_used_percent` (later) — newest datapoint **17:40Z**. Nothing for ~49 minutes.
- `gerrit_healthy` (later still) — **no datapoints at all**.

This explains, with one mechanism, what has been recorded as three separate mysteries:

- `illbred-sour-alpaca` — alarms firing on healthy operation. The empty buckets are not "cadence
  aliasing"; they are the section never running. With `treat_missing_data = "breaching"` and
  `datapoints_to_alarm = 2` of 3, a late-section metric alarms permanently.
- `enviable-beloved-buffalo` — "three rebar/host metrics have published nothing for 7+ days". Those
  metrics are late in the script. They have not been failing to publish; they have never been reached.
- The dead-man design from `herbal-garish-monkey` is sound in principle but is being fed by a
  publisher that silently truncates itself.

Measured consequence on the live alarm surface: of six alarms in ALARM at 17:09 UTC, only **two** were
genuine breaches. The other four fired on gaps while their values were healthy —
`docker_unaccounted_bytes` read 1.87 GB against a 2 GiB threshold, and BuildKit read 10% against 85.

## Operator consequence, observed first-hand

An orchestrating session was using `mem_used_percent` to decide when to restart a leaking MCP process.
That metric is late in the script, so it went blind for 49 minutes while the leak continued. The
decision had to be made by reading the host directly instead. **A probe that truncates itself removes
exactly the signals an operator reaches for during pressure**, because pressure is what makes the
probe slow enough to be killed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The blocking call is identified by measurement, not inference — per-section timing that names
      which call consumes the wall-clock gap between ~35s CPU and 4min elapsed.
- [ ] The probe completes within its timeout under representative load, demonstrated over consecutive
      runs rather than once. State the margin.
- [ ] A truncated run cannot be silent: if the probe is killed or exits early, that fact is itself
      published or alarmed, so "the section never ran" is distinguishable from "the value is missing".
      Today they are identical, which is what made this take a day to find.
- [ ] Metric publication no longer depends on position in the script — either sections are ordered so
      no metric can be starved, or each publishes independently of the others' progress. State which.
- [ ] Defect-seeded: force a blocking call to exceed the timeout and confirm the new truncation signal
      fires and the surviving metrics are correctly attributed.
- [ ] Re-measure the alarm surface afterwards: the four alarms shown above as firing-on-gaps should
      clear without their thresholds changing. If they do not, the diagnosis is incomplete.
- [ ] Portability: host shell + systemd + local validation; no dependence on any single CI provider.

## Testing

1. RED first: instrument the current probe and show a run exceeding 4 minutes with ~35s CPU, killed
   at the boundary.
2. Confirm which metrics fall after the kill point and that they match the observed absences.
3. After the fix, verify late-section metrics publish on consecutive runs, including under induced
   I/O load.

## Provenance

Found 2026-09-05 while investigating why `mem_used_percent` had stopped publishing. Earlier in the
same session the gaps were repeatedly mis-attributed to "cadence jitter" and "sparse publishing" —
including by me — because a truncated run and a slow publisher are indistinguishable from the metric
side. The journal is what settles it.
data.title: The observability probe blocks on I/O, exceeds its 4-minute systemd timeout and is SIGTERM-ed mid-run, so every metric published after the kill point never appears — this is the root cause of the "sparse publishing" behind the dead-man alarms
